description: Two interviews from the same job/resume but different answer quality must produce a materially different OUTCOME - specifically, whether the interview terminates via sufficient_evidence_collected - not necessarily a different raw competency-choice sequence (see expected_behavior for why raw sequence comparison is unreliable).

answer_texts: I built a Django REST API with JWT authentication, wrote pytest suites at 90% coverage, and used SQLAlchemy with connection pooling for performance.
I optimize slow queries by running EXPLAIN ANALYZE to find sequential scans, then add covering indexes on the filtered/joined columns - cut a 2s query to 50ms on a production Postgres table this way.

To go deeper on that same system: I configured SQLAlchemy's QueuePool explicitly with a max overflow tuned to our traffic, wrote integration tests that exercise the actual SQL queries end-to-end (not just mocks), and used EXPLAIN ANALYZE in CI to catch a missing index before it ever reached production.

One more concrete example from that project: I profiled a slow endpoint with cProfile, found it was doing an N+1 query pattern in the Django ORM, rewrote it with select_related and a covering index on the join column, and verified with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the sequential scan was gone - cut p95 latency from 800ms to 45ms.
I mean, I've used Python a bit, not really sure what else to say about it.
It's kind of hard to explain, I guess I just wrote some code at some point.

expected_behavior: P8B.5 root-cause finding (traced deterministically in MOCK mode, zero LLM variance, before ever attributing anything to real-model behavior - see the P8B.5 report): the original check (`sequence_differs_by_answer_quality`, comparing raw per-turn competency choices) is NOT a reliable signal for this fixture and was replaced, not weakened - it was testing an assumption the production contract does not actually make. utils/adaptive_interview.py's competency_priority()/_uncertainty_factor() deliberately prioritize BREADTH before DEPTH (P3 Phase 6 'question diversity'): a never-asked competency always has uncertainty 1.0 (undamped), while an asked-but-insufficient competency's uncertainty is at most 1.0 MINUS a diversity penalty that only grows - so with two equal-weight competencies (Python, SQL here), the engine deterministically opens the untouched one at step 2 REGARDLESS of how weak the step-1 answer was. This was verified in mock mode: both scenarios produce [Python, SQL, ...] as their first two turns, exactly as the code intends - not a bug, and not model variance. Given that, the raw sequence can coincidentally match between a strong-answer and a weak-answer run purely from this deterministic tie-break, independent of answer quality. The RELIABLE signal for 'does answer quality change the outcome' is whether the interview reaches sufficient_evidence_collected - MIN_CONFIDENCE_FOR_COVERAGE and evidence_status=='supported' are exactly the mechanism answer quality is SUPPOSED to drive. Scenario A's two genuinely strong, detailed answers (covering both Python and SQL) should terminate the interview via sufficient_evidence_collected; scenario B's three genuinely vague/evasive answers (bounded to max_questions=3) should NOT, precisely because 'insufficient'/low-confidence evidence never clears the coverage threshold. The underlying contract (answer quality must materially affect the interview's outcome) is unchanged and, if anything, now checked more rigorously - previously a fixture could coincidentally PASS via a sequence-length artifact without genuinely proving anything about answer quality. P8B.5 FINAL root cause (classification C - genuine real-model limitation - and therefore reclassified to bucket B): after the checks above were corrected, this case was run against real Groq FOUR times with byte-identical fixtures and produced pass, fail, fail across runs - i.e. genuinely NON-DETERMINISTIC, which definitively rules out the earlier fixture-fragility theory (adding more/stronger reinforcing answer content did NOT make it deterministic). The real cause is that this check is gated on MIN_CONFIDENCE_FOR_COVERAGE (config/settings.py = 0.65) being cleared by the MODEL's self-reported `confidence` field, and openai/gpt-oss-20b's confidence calibration is conservative and stochastic: it frequently returns 0.6-ish even for genuinely strong, detailed, concrete answers (directly observed: a diagnostic call returned confidence=0.6). Whether a run clears 0.65 is therefore a coin-flip on model calibration, not a measure of whether the ADAPTIVE ENGINE is correct. MIN_CONFIDENCE_FOR_COVERAGE was deliberately NOT lowered - tuning a production threshold to make a benchmark pass would be weakening real product behavior to accommodate one model's calibration, which this project explicitly forbids. Instead this case is now bucket B: the termination/coverage logic it exercises is deterministic Python business logic gated on a numeric threshold, and testing it requires CONTROLLED confidence inputs, exactly like the already-bucket-B integrity severity-cap case (which is likewise gated on a scripted confidence value). The answer_texts remain realistic (an improvement over the original placeholders, and correct under both providers) even though this case no longer consumes real-provider calls.

answer_texts: I designed a high-throughput data pipeline in Python using asyncio for concurrent I/O, implemented custom connection pooling, wrote unit and integration tests with pytest, and profiled with cProfile to cut processing time by 60%.
I also wrote a full pytest suite with fixtures and mocks for that pipeline, set up CI to run it on every commit, and used type hints with mypy to catch integration bugs before they reached staging.

expected_behavior: Terminates via sufficient_evidence_collected after strong Python answers. P8B.5 root-cause finding: a real Groq run of the single-answer version of this fixture reported termination_reason=None even after the P8B Batch 3 content fix (realistic answer text, not a placeholder) - confirmed via a fresh live run (see the P8B.5 report). Root cause classified D (fixture-design fragility, not a code/prompt defect): the fixture bet everything on ONE real-model confidence score clearing the exact MIN_CONFIDENCE_FOR_COVERAGE (0.65) threshold, with no way to reinforce it if that single judgment landed just under the bar - real-model confidence on any one call is not perfectly calibrated/deterministic (openai/gpt-oss-20b, temperature 0.7). Since this job has only ONE competency, there is no breadth-first competitor to distract the engine (unlike interviewer_adaptive_sequence_differs_by_answer_quality) - record_answer's competency_confidence uses a running MAX across answers for the same competency, so a second, equally strong, genuinely different Python answer gives the engine a legitimate, contract-consistent second chance to clear the threshold (via decide_next_action's own 'probe' action on the same competency) without inventing any new expected behavior. The check/contract itself (must terminate via sufficient_evidence_collected once genuinely well-supported) is unchanged. P8B.5 FINAL root cause (classification C, reclassified to bucket B - supersedes the fixture-fragility theory above): the two-answer version PASSED one live run and then FAILED a later one with byte-identical fixtures, reporting termination_reason='no_further_progress_possible' - i.e. the engine correctly exhausted MAX_FOLLOW_UPS_PER_COMPETENCY (2) probing Python without the model's self-reported confidence ever clearing MIN_CONFIDENCE_FOR_COVERAGE (0.65) across THREE separate strong answers. That non-determinism proves the blocker is openai/gpt-oss-20b's conservative, stochastic confidence calibration (frequently ~0.6 even for concrete, detailed answers), not the fixture and not the engine - the engine's behavior in that run was exactly correct per its documented contract. MIN_CONFIDENCE_FOR_COVERAGE was deliberately NOT lowered to force a pass. This case is now bucket B for the same reason as the integrity severity-cap case: it tests deterministic threshold logic that requires CONTROLLED confidence inputs to exercise meaningfully.
